notes.text: For more than 8, cook the chicken and egg in two skillets side by side, with half of everything in each.

callback.body: You've simmered before: small, lazy bubbles that cook food gently. Oyakodon simmers chicken in a sweet soy broth, then uses that same gentle heat, and a lid, to set eggs on top.

move.title: Simmer, then set
move.body: Oyakodon is a Japanese rice bowl. Its name means "parent and child," because it has chicken and egg. Today you'll simmer onion and chicken in a sweet soy broth, pour beaten eggs over the top, and cover the pan so they set gently. Then it all goes over rice, broth and all.

why.title: Gentle bubbles, juicy chicken
why.body: Hard boiling squeezes chicken tight and pushes its juice out, so it turns tough and stringy. A gentle simmer cooks it through slowly and keeps it juicy. If the bubbles get big and rolling, turn the heat down.

why.title: The broth is the sauce
why.body: Japanese cooks make this broth with dashi, a stock made from dried fish and seaweed. Chicken broth works well too. Soy sauce makes it salty, and mirin and sugar make it sweet. It soaks into the rice underneath, so the rice is full of flavor.

why.title: Beat the eggs just a little
why.body: Stir the eggs only until the yolks break up, leaving streaks of white and yellow. In the pan they set into soft ribbons of both colors. Beaten smooth, they'd turn into one flat yellow layer.

why.title: The lid cooks the top
why.body: The bottom of the egg sits in the hot broth, but the top only gets heat from the steam. The lid traps that steam, so the top sets without anyone flipping it.

wrong.fix: Turn the heat down until only small bubbles rise. The chicken stays tender that way.

wrong.sign: The egg is still runny on top
wrong.fix: Put the lid back on and give it another minute, then check with the thermometer again.
Add a few tablespoons of broth or water. Next time, keep the heat lower.
Serve it with more rice. Next time, use a little less soy sauce.

quiz.q: Why keep the broth at a gentle simmer instead of a hard boil?
choices: Hard boiling makes the chicken tough
quiz.explain: Gentle heat cooks chicken through and keeps it juicy.

quiz.q: Why cover the pan after the eggs go in?
choices: The trapped steam sets the top of the eggs
To keep the eggs a secret
quiz.explain: The lid holds in steam, which cooks the top of the egg without flipping it.

substitutions.note: Use half as much rice vinegar as mirin, and add 1 extra teaspoon of sugar for every tablespoon of vinegar.

steps.text: Put the rice in the saucepan and cover it with cold water. Swish it with your hand, then carefully pour off the cloudy water, holding the rice back with your hand. Do this 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the rice cooks up fluffy instead of gluey.

steps.text: Add {qty:water} of water to the rice. Bring it to a boil over high heat with the lid off. Then turn the heat to low, put the lid on, and cook without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: When the timer rings, turn off the burner and leave the lid on. The rice keeps steaming while you finish.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half through the root, peel it, and slice each half into thin half-moons.
steps.tip: Lay each half flat side down so it can't roll.

steps.text: Slice the green onions into thin rings.
Crack the {n:egg} eggs into the medium bowl. Stir them with the fork just until the yolks break up, about 10 stirs. Streaks of white are what you want.
Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.
steps.tip: Raw egg can carry germs. Clean hands before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Cut the chicken into bite-size pieces, about 1 inch. Leave them on the cutting board.
Wash your hands and the knife with hot, soapy water.
Pour the chicken broth, soy sauce, and mirin into the skillet and add the sugar. Add the onion. Bring it to a simmer over medium heat and cook until the onion is soft.
Lift the cutting board over the pan and slide the chicken into the broth with the back of the knife. Spread it out in one layer.
steps.tip: Slide it in low and slowly, so the broth doesn't splash.

steps.text: Wash your hands, the knife, and the cutting board with hot, soapy water.
Simmer gently, turning the chicken over with the wooden spoon halfway through, until it's cooked all the way through.
steps.look: Small, steady bubbles, and the chicken is white all over.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece of chicken. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, simmer 2 more minutes and check again.
Turn the heat to low. Pour the eggs over the chicken in a slow circle, starting in the middle and spiraling out. Don't stir. Put the lid on.
steps.look: The egg is soft but set, with no clear, runny parts.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer sideways into the thickest part of the egg. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, cover it again for 1 more minute and check again.
Turn off the stove. Fluff the rice and spoon it into bowls. Cut the egg and chicken into portions with the wooden spoon and slide one onto each bowl with some broth. Sprinkle with green onions.
steps.tip: Use the ladle to add a little extra broth to each bowl. The rice soaks it up.
